item.title: “Monks, suppose there is a bitter gourd mixed with poison. Then a man comes who desires to live, not to die, who desires happiness and…
item.description:
“Monks, suppose there is a bitter gourd mixed with poison. Then a man comes who desires to live, not to die, who desires happiness and loathes suffering. Someone says to him: ‘Good man, this bitter gourd is mixed with poison. If you wish, eat it. While eating, you will not find delight in its color, smell, or taste. After eating, you may meet death or deadly suffering.’ That man might eat it without reflection, without refusal. While eating, he does not find delight in its color, smell, or taste. After eating, he meets death or deadly suffering. Monks, I say that this course of practice is like that simile — namely, a course of practice that is painful in the present and also has painful results in the future.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 46 – Mahādhammasamādānasutta

item.title: “Monks, there are these three fires. What three? The fire of greed, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion. These, monks, are the three…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these three fires. What three? The fire of greed, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion. These, monks, are the three fires.

The fire of greed burns up people
Who are intoxicated by sensual pleasures.
The fire of hatred burns up
Those who are hateful,
Who kill living beings.

The fire of delusion burns up
Those who are confused,
Not trained in the noble Dhamma.
Not understanding these fires,
People delight in personal existence.

They increase hell,
The realm of animals,
The domain of hungry ghosts,
And also the asuras —
They are not freed
From Māra’s bondage.”

From: Itivuttaka 93

item.title: “Here, monks, the second kind of ascetics and brahmins think: ‘These first ascetics and brahmins, entering and indulging, ate the bait … and have not…
item.description:
“Here, monks, the second kind of ascetics and brahmins think: ‘These first ascetics and brahmins, entering and indulging, ate the bait … and have not escaped Māra’s power. Suppose we completely abandon the bait and the world’s offerings, abandon what is fearful, go into the forest and dwell.’ They completely abandon the bait and the world’s offerings, abandon what is fearful, go into the forest and dwell. There they become grass-eaters, millet-eaters, raw-rice eaters, Nivara-seed eaters, crust-eaters, husk-eaters, rice-scum eaters, sesame-seed eaters, grass-eaters, cow-dung eaters, forest roots and fruits eaters, fallen-fruit eaters. At the end of the summer, when water and grass become scarce, their bodies become extremely emaciated. Because their bodies become extremely emaciated, their energy for striving is exhausted. Because their energy is exhausted, their mind’s liberation is exhausted. Because their mind’s liberation is exhausted, they return to the bait cast by Māra and the world’s offerings. There they again enter, indulge, and eat those foods. By entering, indulging, and eating, they become infatuated; from infatuation, heedless; from heedlessness, subject to Māra’s will. Thus, monks, these second ascetics and brahmins have not escaped Māra’s power.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 25 – Nivāpasutta

item.title: “Monks, here a monk, reflecting wisely, does not consent to arisen sensual thought; he abandons, dispels, destroys, makes it non-existent. He does not consent to…
item.description:
“Monks, here a monk, reflecting wisely, does not consent to arisen sensual thought; he abandons, dispels, destroys, makes it non-existent. He does not consent to arisen ill-will thought … does not consent to arisen harmful thought; he abandons, dispels, destroys, makes it non-existent. He does not consent to any arisen evil, unwholesome states; he abandons, dispels, destroys, makes them non-existent.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 2 – Sabbāsavasutta

item.title: “This good teaching I give to you — You who have gathered here. Dig up the root of craving Like digging up birana grass. Do…
item.description:
“This good teaching I give to you —
You who have gathered here.
Dig up the root of craving
Like digging up birana grass.
Do not let Māra destroy you,
Like a flood destroying reeds.”

“Even though a tree is cut down,
If its root remains uncut,
The tree grows back —
So too, if the latent tendency to craving is not uprooted,
Suffering arises again and again.”

“The thirty-six streams of craving
Sweep away a person who is bent on pleasing thoughts —
Thoughts of lust,
Sweeping him away with wrong view.”

From: Dhammapada 334-359

item.title: The inner fetter and the outer fetter — Beings are entangled in these fetters. I ask Gotama about this: Who can escape these fetters? (The…
item.description:
The inner fetter and the outer fetter —
Beings are entangled in these fetters.
I ask Gotama about this:
Who can escape these fetters?

(The Blessed One):
One established in virtue, wise,
Developing mind and wisdom,
Ardent and discreet —
That monk can escape the fetters.
One who has abandoned greed,
Hatred, and ignorance,
The defilement-free arahant —
He has escaped the fetters.
Where name-and-form is destroyed
Without remainder,
Where the hindrance and perceptions of form are destroyed —
There the fetters are cut.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.23

item.title: Elder Parāpariya: Most bodies, Full of pus and blood, Are made by skilled people Into beautifully painted boxes. Bitter as sweetness, Suffering bound by the…
item.description:
Elder Parāpariya:

Most bodies,
Full of pus and blood,
Are made by skilled people
Into beautifully painted boxes.

Bitter as sweetness,
Suffering bound by the agreeable —
Like a sharp sword smeared with honey —
The greedy person does not know.

One who lusts after female form,
Female taste, female touch,
One who is infatuated by female smell,
Meets many sufferings.

All the streams from women —
Five kinds flow in five places —
A person with energy and strength
Can block them.

One who has a goal, abiding in Dhamma,
Skilled, clear-seeing,
Rejoices in doing the duty
Connected with Dhamma and meaning.

Sunk in temporary benefits,
Abandon what is unbeneficial.
If one thinks of such a thing,
Not the thing to be done —
That one, not heedless,
Sees clearly.

If it is a good deed to do,
Rejoice in practicing the Dhamma.
Seize the doing immediately —
That is truly the highest happiness.

With high and low means,
Deceiving others,
Killing, causing sorrow,
Violent, overpowering others —

As a strong man carves wood,
Driving out a peg with a peg,
So the good person,
Drives out a sense-faculty with a sense-faculty.

Developing faith, energy, concentration,
Training mindfulness and wisdom,
Using five to conquer five,
Stainless, one goes forward.

That brahmin, having a goal,
Abiding in Dhamma,
Following the Buddha’s instruction,
Complete, with full strength —
That person enjoys peace.

From: Theragāthā 16.2

item.title: “Monks, what one intends, what one plans, and what one has a tendency towards — that becomes a basis for the establishment of consciousness. When…
item.description:
“Monks, what one intends, what one plans, and what one has a tendency towards — that becomes a basis for the establishment of consciousness. When there is a basis, there is an establishment of consciousness. When consciousness is established and grows, there is a production of future renewed existence. When there is future renewed existence, future birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.38

item.title: Elder Siṅgālapitar: “Look at the forest of Bhesakaḷā! A monk lives there, Heir to the Buddha’s teaching, Pervading this great earth With the perception of…
item.description:
Elder Siṅgālapitar:
“Look at the forest of Bhesakaḷā!
A monk lives there,
Heir to the Buddha’s teaching,
Pervading this great earth
With the perception of a skeleton.
I think that monk will quickly
Abandon sensual lust.”

From: Theragāthā 1.18

item.title: "O great king, when the eye sees a form, the monk does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes…
item.description:
"O great king, when the eye sees a form, the monk does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the eye faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — that cause the monk restrains, guards the eye faculty, practices the restraint of the eye faculty."

From: Dīgha Nikāya 2 – Sāmaññaphalasutta
